yesterday. and yet time is running out, ladies and gentlemen. we are now one week away from the european council and a few days from the date of 31 october, which was agreed with the previous government for the united kingdom's exit from the european union in an orderly fashion which is much better, as you said, than a disorderly exit. why aren't we there? because the british proposals raise three major problems. firstly, on the question of the border and control of property on the island of ireland. prime minister johnson rejected on arrival - we know that - the backstop, which is the kind of insurance or safety net that we had agreed with the theresa may government. that's a fact. at the same time, prime minister johnson recognises that regulatory alignment for goods is essential between northern ireland and the european union and we obviously agree on this. on the other hand, to solve the problem of customs controls, the united kingdom is simply proposing that we take a legal commitment together, in the international treaty that will bind us, to avoid, under any circumstances, customs or regulatory controls and any physical infrastructure at the border between ireland and northern ireland. of course, we share this objective, which is one of the objectives of the backstop: that there should be no border, no infrastructure. but what we are really being asked to do is to accept a system which is not developed, which is not tested, of controls scattered over the island of ireland and that would be largely based on exemptions, derogations from the european customs code, technologies which remain to be developed, changes to international law which are provided for by the common transit convention and finally a new compliance system but without the guarantees which are provided for by the protocol. ladies and gentlemen, we need customs controls, serious and rigorous regulatory controls everywhere, outside, at the external border of the single market and our customs union. in ireland, as elsewhere, we need operational controls, real controls, credible controls. it is the credibility of the single market that is at stake and therefore the credibility vis-à-vis consumers, businesses and also, we do not forget, third countries with which we are negotiating agreements. that's the first point of disagreement. the second point concerns the legitimate requirement to find legally operational solutions. with the protocol we have established a safety net which clarifies the regime applicable on the island of ireland and this safety net is legally operational as it would apply until and unless we find an alternative solution. by proposing to abolish this safety net, to abolish the backstop and to look for alternative solutions during the transition period, that is to say later, the british proposal does not give us the security of the protocol. one example: there is no real solution for small and mediumsized enterprises in these british proposals, except to propose a general derogation. second example: what would happen if the joint committee, to which the british want to refer all the questions that are not answered at the moment, could not reach an agreement during the transition? the uk projections suggest that the solution would then depend on unilateral measures to be taken by the uk or the eu. there would then, of course, be a significant risk to the integrity of the single market, since the uk proposals would also commit us to never having border controls between ireland and northern ireland, which would become two separate jurisdictions. the third point of disagreement, as i speak, is obviously the british proposal on consent. we have always regretted the absence of stormont for the last two and a half years to give a strong and strong northern irish voice in our negotiations. in the existing protocol, we have provided with the british mechanisms which allow northern ireland to be represented. we are ready to look again at new ideas for a greater role for the northern irish institutions in implementing the protocol in accordance with the good friday belfast agreement. but today the british proposal, as it is on the table, is simply to make the implementation of the protocol conditional on a unilateral decision by the institutions of northern ireland, which could then decide unilaterally, from the outset, the day after the ratification of the withdrawal agreement by your assembly and the house of commons, not to activate the proposed solution for northern ireland at all. and if it were still activated, the northern irish authorities could decide every four years to challenge it. ladies and gentlemen, the british government's proposal today, as it stands and which we cannot accept, would replace an operational, practical, legal solution with a hypothetical and provisional solution. finally, there is a fourth point which is really problematic, which is not the withdrawal agreement but the political declaration, which is next to the withdrawal agreement and is very important, because it describes what will happen after brexit, with an agreement, i hope, and even without an agreement, it is not a destination, it will have to be rebuilt with the united kingdom, everything that has been torn apart 44 years of integration and cooperation, it will have to be rebuilt a relationship in all areas: trade, security, universities, fisheries, aviation, police and judicial cooperation, defence and security. and we are outlining with the uk government the other options, which we left open in the political declaration. it also asks us to remove the references agreed with theresa may on a very important point, which is the level playing field, that is to say a basic rule of the game, a basis of fairness and rules of the game in taxation, state aid, social rights, environmental rights, consumer rights. so, we are faced with this demand. the second agreement approved by the european council for the withdrawal of the united kingdom from the eu corresponds in substance to the agreement reached in 2018, with amendments to aspects related to customs controls, taxation and movement and control of goods, relating to northern ireland. in a context of still uncertain outcome, we reaffirm four central premises of our analysis and positioning. more than three years have passed since the referendum which dictated the sovereign decision of the british people to leave the eu, and it has yet to be implemented. the fundamental question is respect for the will of the british people. the uk's withdrawal from the eu should not be used to call into question labour and social rights, either in the uk or in eu member states, in the name of alleged future adjustments or impacts. the rights of migrant workers, which are not ensured by the mere application of the eu acquis (as demonstrated by the agreement reached with david cameron in 2016), must be strongly defended and ensured, including through negotiations on a bilateral plan of relations between states. measures should be taken to develop a framework of mutually beneficial bilateral relations with the united kingdom, respecting the sovereignty of states and the rights of peoples.

in writing. in the process of preparing the general budget for the financial year 2020, parliament has played and must continue to play a decisive role in ensuring that the european union is able to meet increasingly complex challenges. among these, i would particularly stress the need to provide the gai agencies and the european public prosecutor's office with the appropriate resources, staff and training to enable them to carry out their assigned tasks effectively. the year 2020, like previous years, is expected to be particularly challenging in terms of security, migration, protection of fundamental rights and respect for the rule of law. the gis agencies have been at the forefront of responding to these crises so far, demonstrating a high capacity to adapt to the changing european context. europol and eurojust also make an important contribution to the fight against organised and transnational crime, drug trafficking and financial crime. the european public prosecutor's office will also need to have the necessary means to conduct thorough investigations and prosecute cross-border criminal activities. the guarantee of rights, legality, security and the protection of the financial interests of the union are objectives which we must ensure in the adoption of the budget.
in writing. i would like to draw attention to a number of problems that i have identified in the general budget of the european union for the financial year 2020. the first concerns the under-spending of youth programmes and this should be changed in the future. it is the young who will be responsible for our countries and our union in the future. the priority of every budget should be to increase the funding for good education for young people and the creation of new jobs. it's a pity that it's not always like that. for example, the 'erasmus+' programme continues to be highly regarded and very popular, with applications far exceeding the available funds. this should be replaced by more funding to enable more people to benefit from the scheme. another very important issue is the need to increase funding for the european labour authority (ela). this should become a priority for the union as the youth unemployment rate, which stood at 14,2% in april 2019, remains unacceptably high and is particularly serious in most of the new eu member states. clearly, more eu funding is needed to increase the employment opportunities of young people and to strengthen their entrepreneurship, as well as to combat unemployment. these clearly defined priorities are missing from the general budget for the following year.
rapporteur. – madam president, first i would like also to thank the court of auditors, the commission, the agencies network and parliament’s staff for their valuable work during the 2017 discharge procedure. we are today discussing the last discharges from that year. the decentralised agencies are highly visible in the member states and have a direct impact on the daily lives of the union’s citizens. this is especially the case for the european asylum support office (easo). the refugee crisis has shaken europe from 2015 and even though, in the light of statistics, the crisis seems to be under control we still have to ensure the durability of our asylum system to avoid new crises from being born in the future. that is exactly why the money spent from the eu budget has to be used efficiently and any fraud in the use of public money has to be prevented. unfortunately, in the case of easo, this was not the fact for the financial year 2017. the european court of auditors issued an unqualified audit opinion on the reliability of the accounts and on the legality and regularity of the revenue and the payments underlying the accounts for all agencies in 2017 except for the payments of easo. we do regret that the court issued an adverse opinion for easo’s payments. the matters which led the court to issue this opinion were mainly related to non-compliance of payments on public procurement and recruitment procedures. therefore, in march 2019, the european parliament decided to postpone granting discharge to the executive director of easo for the financial year in question and to postpone the closure of the accounts for that year. as the discharge authority, the committee on budgetary control proposes, after an almost unanimous vote, to finally refuse the discharge of easo for the financial year 2017. the following issues were taken into consideration: first, the findings of olaf regarding irregularities surrounding the breach of procurement procedures, misappropriation of union funds, mismanagement, abuse of position in human resources issues, breaches of data protection rules, harassment and inappropriate behaviour towards staff; second, the systematic nature of non—compliance has demonstrated an inadequate internal control system; and third, the combined error from non—compliant payments amounted to at least eur 7.7 million, corresponding to 10.3% of the total payments made by easo in 2017. in addition, we must highlight that the budget for the financial year 2017 was implemented under the supervision of the office’s previous management and that this report concerns the discharge procedure for that year. however, we do acknowledge easo’s new management’s commitment to ambitious reforms. we recognise the progress made on the implementation of internal control systems. all in all, we cannot compromise good governance and sound financial management of the eu budget. i hope that this parliament will not do that. with such grave findings as the case of easo in 2017, refusing to grant discharge is the only way forward.
member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i should like to begin by thanking mr sarvamaa, who was rapporteur, for his valuable work. i believe that he has thoroughly studied and worked on the easo matter and the 2017 financial year. firstly, easo plays a key role in the field of our european migration policy and in the field of advising member states on their migration policy. easo is making a very valuable contribution to the establishment of a european asylum system. and we are in the middle of this and we want to take further steps where easo will play a more and more important role. and that requires building on trust and solidarity on the ground. easo is a partner of the member states, supporting their asylum systems, which are faced with a high number of asylum applications. easo is also an important service provider for the rapid resettlement of migrants who are voluntarily admitted by member states. in order to ensure convergence of national asylum systems, easo has developed standards for reception conditions that are intended to apply throughout europe. member states have the right and undertake to use the expertise of easo, for example in relation to the situation in the countries of origin, where easo can provide comprehensive information. the importance of the work of this agency is one of the reasons why the commission takes the issue of easo's governance and past problems very seriously. it is about the authority of easo, which is necessary. the commission has been closely monitoring the situation of easo since 2016 and has supported efforts to improve the governance and functioning of the agency, to learn from and to rectify errors, with particular emphasis on recruitment, procurement, budgetary and audit procedures and internal governance. the commission has also provided the easo with a number of documents, including the easo's annual report on the implementation of the schengen acquis, the annual report on the implementation of the schengen acquis and the annual report on the implementation of the schengen acquis. we will continue to do so. but we must all be clear about one thing: we have two types of agencies in the european union. the first type are executive agencies which are ultimately part of the commission's mission, where the oversight is clarified. and we have decentralized agencies, which are exactly what we want because of secondary european law. the legal structure is exactly what we wanted, and the commission has very, very limited co-responsibility here. the main responsibility lies with the management board, which includes representatives of all member states the commission has only two seats and the main responsibility lies with the management itself. in fact, these decentralised agencies are somewhere in the triangle between the council, parliament and the commission, and there is no clear technical supervision, no clear in-house supervision, no clear supervisory function, no clear legal supervision. i would also like to make the following proposal to the council, after my experience of the last ten years and just before i leave the house: i think we should learn from this case of a misdevelopment in these decentralised agencies - especially as they have gained enormous importance in recent years - and come to a clear technical supervision, a clear service supervision, a clear legal supervision. it is not clear whether this will be the commission. but if you are in doubt, you need an authority that is operational 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and that takes care of this task and therefore also ensures that the rules are followed and that the guarantee is given. if it is primarily the responsibility of the agency itself to remedy deficiencies, then there is a certain bias at the bottom. i think that, ladies and gentlemen, our common task should be to reflect on this - apart from the individual case - as a lesson to be drawn from this case. back to the case: we welcome the considerable progress made in working with the management board and the interim director. 48 of the 61 actions provided for in the action plan have already been completed to address the shortcomings identified by the european court of auditors. it is about strengthening procurement procedures, it is about internal controls, and it is also about speeding up recruitment. progress was made in recruitment in 2019, with 100 out of 175 recruitments made that year and nine management positions filled, with only six remaining vacant. we trust that the new executive director, nina gregori, who took office a few months ago, will consolidate the work and ensure that all recommendations are fully implemented, thus fully restoring easo's credibility. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of all measures. following the report of olaf, our anti-fraud authority, the commission will support the implementation of the recommendations concerning the responsibilities of the management board as the appointing authority in relation to the agency in this capacity. our common objective must be to put in place measures to prevent incidents of this kind from ever happening again. the commission relies in particular on the management of easo to ensure the proper functioning of the agency. we are prepared to continue to provide our expertise here. in order to help tackle the challenges of asylum, we proposed three years ago to transform easo into a fully-fledged european asylum agency to better fulfil its mandate. we therefore call on parliament and the member states to give priority to our proposals for change, so that we can adopt this legislation quickly.

member of the commission. the commission is not i would like to thank everyone in this chamber for their overwhelming support for a credible accession process and in particular for giving the green light to the two countries, north macedonia and albania, to start accession negotiations. we are not talking about them joining tomorrow or the day after, but we are talking about a process that will take several years. it can take years to build credibility, and it can take minutes or hours to destroy it. this has happened to some extent in the western balkans, but i'm telling you, not just in the western balkans. with this decision we have lost a great deal of the credibility, the reliability, the predictability that we stand for, that we advocate and fight for worldwide, as the european union. i say this in the light of the fact that a whole series of problems are reappearing in our immediate neighbourhood. the european union has a duty to help the people of the middle east, and to help the people of the middle east. i can only hope that those responsible for this current situation did not realise, in taking this decision, what it means for the european union's standing on a global scale and particularly in the neighbourhood, to have lost its capacity to find solutions, its influence and its power of enforcement. it's not gonna be easy to get that back. i am inclined - because i am a member of the party of the glass half full - to believe that things will turn out well again, and i am also prepared to take seriously the various arguments put forward in recent months to justify why the negotiations should not be opened now. i also admit that i sometimes felt that arguments were being put forward here which were really an excuse to avoid having to say clearly and unequivocally: i am against enlargement. one of the arguments we heard from france, but also from one or another country, was that we need to deepen, improve our form of cooperation, decision-making and so on before the next enlargement. i personally say: yes, i understand a lot about this, but i do not understand that these processes take place one after the other, but it is quite possible, sensible, realistic and pragmatic to run these processes in parallel, because both will take years. the only thing is that if we talk first about deepening and then about further accessions, then these countries have an accession perspective that is set in the 1930s, and i think we can agree that there is no perspective in this context. i can also assure you, ladies and gentlemen, that my services - myself, and, i assume, my successor - will be very keen to look at the methodology of the accession process. nobody is perfect. there are always possibilities for improvement, but much of what i have heard so far already exists, it already exists: the emphasis on the rule of law, the possibility of suspending negotiations, and no negotiation leads to 'necessarily' accession, but also this process is reversible. so that's what we're going to do, and i hope you'll participate in this issue with the commitment that you've brought to this issue. and so i'm going to end with a little story that's much shorter than it sounds: in 2013, as a regional commissioner in brussels, i organised a small seminar with civil society representatives from northern ireland, who presented their various examples, projects, case studies, how they organised, operated and promoted reconciliation in northern ireland. i can tell you that 90% of the participants in 2013 were representatives of the countries of the former yugoslavia. and they'll know exactly why they've been involved. because they are fully aware that peace, stability and prosperity in the western balkans region can only be achieved by integrating it into a larger whole, namely the european union. i would like to thank you again for this strong signal of hope, which you will send tomorrow with the relevant resolution, and i wish the president of the parliament of north macedonia all the best and thank him personally for the many initiatives he has taken in recent months to open up the country to europe.

- good afternoon. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to greet the presidents of parliament who have preceded me and who are here with us today, in particular president enrique barón crespo, who was in office on the day the berlin wall fell. thirty years ago, germany and europe were living through one of the most important and significant pages in their recent history. after decades of suffering, the lacerating wound of the division of germany and europe was finding its composition through the fall of its most obvious and odious symbol. finally, the wall fell under the pressure of thousands of women and men, eager to regain their freedom and dignity after years of oppression and deprivation of their basic rights. i would like to remind you that the success of that night was the result of president of the german bundestag. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. nothing has to stay the way it is. on november 9, 1989, i realized what that meant. the will of my countrymen for freedom in the gdr was stronger than the berlin wall. thirty years ago, citizens throughout central and eastern europe took their destiny into their own hands. the transformative force that unfolded reached what for decades seemed inevitable: the fall of the berlin wall, the tearing down of the iron curtain across europe. anyone who has ever lived through this moment will never forget it. and those who see the images of that time still feel the power of the emotions that are associated with it, this moment of happiness, a historical moment that stands alone. "we are flying into history" that's what the pilot of an american plane said to his passengers before landing in berlin on the evening of november 9th. he couldn't keep the incredible news of the open battleships to himself, and he had a sense of their scale. the germans in the gdr, the people throughout central and eastern europe are liberating themselves from communist rule, from the soviet union's claim to power. nations found themselves back to being really people's republics because in them the citizens really did decide. democracy and the rule of law prevailed, human and civil rights were enshrined, the market economy replaced the planned economy and, although there was no master plan for this, the process of european unification brought together 500 million people in the east and west in a peaceful development for the good. this is unprecedented in history. so we're keeping in mind what's possible when people come together to stand for something. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that is why i am honoured by your invitation and have gladly followed it to speak to you about the fall of the wall and the happy historical turn for all europe about the courage of those who demonstrated in many places in the gdr, who exerted pressure on the rigid state and party leadership at great personal risk, who demanded reforms and freedom rights or who left everything for their freedom and fled to the west in thousands and not least achieved that this revolution in germany remained peaceful, as well as those in most other neighboring states, whether we remember them as samten or as singing revolution. it's amazing how it happened. and it is indeed cause for celebration! in the cold war, on the western side of the iron curtain, sympathy had been extended to dissidents and oppositionists charter 77, solidarność and other civil rights movements, in which the brave few had initially gathered. their example encouraged others until it became the mass protests that swept away the old regimes in 1989/90. the west had a direct hand in this success - not least because of the double decision of nato, which pushed the weakened soviet union to divert and negotiate. the courage of the people in the east and the firmness of the west, both of which helped to bring the cold war to an end 30 years ago. the opening of the wall came as a surprise, but it was not without its precursors: the election of a pole as pope and his powerful visit to his homeland, the powerful polish trade union movement, the candlelight demonstration in bratislava, the 650-kilometre human chain across the baltic and, not least, the great humanitarian gesture of the hungarians at sopron in the summer of 1989 when they arbitrarily opened the border these and other signs pointed to change. father imre kozma of the hungarian malteser aid service, who was caring for refugees from the gdr at the time, summed up the change in people's attitudes during these eventful months: those who had learned to fear suddenly no longer feared. not even in the gdr. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the legal affairs committee - the body responsible for civil rights in your parliament - met in berlin from 8 to 10 november 1989 in the reichstag building, directly opposite the wall. the european parliament's resolution on the future of the european union and the european union's role in the world is a welcome step towards a new era of peace and stability. they were as unprepared as any of us for an event that would change the world. the parliamentary committee reacted as parliamentary committees do: it adopted an opinion. the declaration states that the events in berlin are to be welcomed. what a contrast to the euphoria of the people! during the night and the following days, hundreds of thousands of people marched, cheering and marveling, through the berlin border crossings, the checkpoints between the gdr and the federal republic. wild strangers were lying in arms 28 years after the wall was built, which was in fact a death strip. at least 140 people lost their lives here. we won't forget them! we do not forget the suffering of their families and the many other victims of the decades of dictatorship in eastern europe. the fact that the members of the european parliament's committee were visibly restraining their joy may also have had something to do with the fact that at the time no one knew whether the wall would finally be history. in our minds - our minds - there were images of the violent repression of the protests: 1953 in the gdr, 1956 in hungary and 1968 in czechoslovakia. the tanks that went off when martial law was imposed in poland in 1981 were still fresh in the minds of the people, and the violent end to the student protests in tiananmen square in beijing in the summer of 1989 was still fresh in the minds of the people. the european events are once again shining in a particularly bright light against this background. the courage of the people, their loud demand for reform, for a voice or for a change of power, had shaken the communist regimes to their foundations. they knew full well the consequences of showing weakness. some continued to believe that they had to prove their strength by being particularly tough. others were no longer able to do so. as different as the citizens' movements were within and between themselves, their criticism of the ruling party, their many voices demanding and expecting political change, all of them were united by the goal of overcoming the lack of freedom: to shake off permanent control, to get rid of arbitrariness, to break down the boundaries, to leave behind the prospects of the imprisoned. who among the young people of europe today can even imagine that for generations real freedom was a dream that seemed impossible to achieve? today, as citizens of the european union, we can freely decide in a large democratic legal area how we live, where we live, study, work and trade. everyone is free to express his opinion, however deviant. the european parliament has been a key player in the fight against racism and xenophobia in the european union. a dream that has come true. we germans know that without european unity, without the desire of europeans to grow together in east and west, there would be no german unity. the one was the prerequisite for the other, both are two sides of the same coin. the four victorious powers made the state unity of germany possible by giving us what we could not claim: their trust. the european community, like our immediate neighbours, has also been able to do so, despite the wounds inflicted on the continent by the second world war unleashed by germany. we germans will never forget this proof of reconciliation! the political change of 1989-90 gave a considerable boost to the process of european unification over the past 30 years. the long-planned single market and economic and monetary union were pushed further, leading to the enlargement of the european union to include the re-established democracies of central and eastern europe. we share the same values that we have long hoped would lead to unchallenged victory. that turned out to be an illusion. instead, our democracies are facing global competition from authoritarian systems that advertise themselves with a high level of efficiency and prosperity, but without giving their citizens what we take for granted in the west: freedom and social justice, progress and sustainability, democracy, the rule of law, universal human rights - all of which make europe worth living in and a place of longing for many people around the world, which by the way still makes authoritarian rulers around the world nervous, because it is obviously still highly attractive. sometimes it seems that we are the ones who doubt it the most. many people - especially those who once took to the streets to demand freedom and expression - are not satisfied, not because they do not value freedom or democracy, but rather because the transitions from dictatorship to democratic compromise are always chaotic, as british historian timothy garton ash once observed. there's pain associated with seizures. what does the west have to offer? this is the question that the polish poet czesław miłosz asked long before the fall of the iron curtain. "freedom from something is a lot, but it is too little, it is much less than freedom to something", he wrote back then. what is freedom to something? we must constantly renegotiate the answer to this question, especially since freedom is not a value in itself. since the french revolution, we have known the triple bottom line: freedom requires equality and fraternity. this too is part of europe's heritage! it meets the needs of the people of europe. they do not live in a single space, but form a community with many different historical traits and national identities. in the west, few people have any idea what it means to have been subjected to dictatorship and foreign rule, sometimes twice. what is known here of the convulsions in which people in all the states of the former eastern bloc had to prove themselves in the years of upheaval that followed? for most people, the freedom gained in the change of system was accompanied by a deep cut, including pretences. while we are talking intensively about immigration issues throughout europe for good reason, people in the eastern parts of our continent are often much more moved by the experience of emigration and its far-reaching consequences. on the other hand, many people sometimes fail to understand the diversity of the original core of europe and the countries that have come together around it. the west is more than just rich and saturated, accustomed to peace and to democracy as a matter of course. the transition to a common europe in east and west remains a major challenge for all of us, especially in the face of the simultaneous rapid changes brought about by globalisation and digitalisation, by global migration and climate change, and by dissolving international obligations. all of this is creating new insecurities and fears in many people. the freedom which prevails in europe today after a century of terrible wars and the loss of humanity in dictatorships is not a mere illusion! it's the side effects, at best, it's actually the freedom of others that causes discomfort and rejection. the liberal europe is enormously diverse. but we still lack a common public, and we lack platforms to share across borders about what is common or what is dividing. it is only through exchanges that we can achieve a genuine pan-european perspective. we can all learn from each other, especially since east germans and eastern europeans are a little ahead of people in the west, because they have 30 years of experience in change processes. this is a valuable experience, especially since we realize that the advances of globalization and digitalization are not stopping anyone. at the political level, we can only really move forward if we perceive and acknowledge each other's perspectives more than before, not to adopt them uncritically, but to understand each other better and to be able to take joint decisions. we always tend to think that our own attitude is the only one that is right. this is the cause of many conflicts in europe. not only that, but sometimes it seems that the gap between east and west is widening. let us not, therefore, jeopardize the greatest achievement of the epochal change of 1989 - that is, the overcoming of the division of our continent! we will all play a role in this rapidly changing world only if we act together, if we defend common positions shared or at least supported by the people of the member states. we will only be able to set the tone and defend our values if we live up to them ourselves. and we will only be taken seriously if we substantially increase our joint efforts to bring stability to the conflict-affected regions within europe and in our neighbourhood. freedom can only be defended by those who know it and live it for themselves and who do not invoke it only on holidays. democracy is as important to the stability of society as wealth and prosperity. our values are the key to curbing the fragmentation of processes and creating a level playing field in global competition. but they are by no means self-evident, and certainly not unchallenged, even in our 21st century. jacques delors has left a warning legacy. he feared that the violent 20th century would bring a new nationalism and a rising individualism. both, he said, threatened the solidarity and social cohesion of the member states of the union, but above all the 'open universalism' and the capacity for tolerance which characterised our shared values and which were europe's heritage. we should remember the words of jacques delors: if the eu fails, this heritage is at risk of being lost. i think the warning is still valid! (applause from the centre) what delors could not have imagined, certainly not wanted: the eu is losing one of its biggest members in a painful process. and our continent is experiencing the return of war and violent border displacement on its eastern border. and even security partners within nato are behaving in ways that even critics of the alliance never thought possible. the rules-based international order is under pressure and this in an increasingly interconnected world where truth no longer counts and national egos are indulged, but where the most pressing questions of world food, migration, climate change and security can only be answered globally. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. this applies to the eu's external relations, but it also applies to the internal european cooperation. europe can only act if the member states cooperate. cohesion is a prerequisite for europe to become 'world-policy-capable', as jean-claude juncker has said. we must overcome narrow-mindedness, narrow-mindedness and fear. the fall of the wall and the 30 years since have shown that nothing has to stay the same. the most massive walls can fall, change is possible if we take them in hand. it's up to us. then europe can learn from the great world change of 1989/90: we are free to act boldly. president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members of parliament, the international day to end impunity for crimes against journalists was established in memory of the death of ghislaine dupont and claude verlon, two french journalists killed while reporting in mali on 2 november 2013. media freedom is an indispensable pillar of our democratic societies. journalists are among the guardians of properly-functioning democracies. they act as public watchdogs, helping to inform and empower citizens. where there is no freedom of speech there is no democracy. for this reason, freedom of expression, media freedom and pluralism are guaranteed in the eu charter of fundamental rights. yet across the globe, journalists face risks and attacks simply for carrying out their work. too often investigations into violence or threats of violence against journalists and media outlets are slow, incomplete and fail to bring the offenders to justice. 31 journalists have been killed worldwide in 2019 alone; more than 800 in the last decade. in 9 out of 10 cases, the killers go unpunished. impunity is the key obstacle to ensuring journalists’ safety, resulting in self-censorship and a chilling effect on the exercise of freedom of expression. the investigations and judicial proceedings following the horrific and unacceptable killings of maltese journalist daphne caruana galizia and slovak journalist ján kuciak have to this day not been concluded. these crimes have shocked european public opinion. the european parliament has made clear in its resolutions on media pluralism and media freedom in the european union that we have a duty to guarantee the freedom of expression and of the press, including the safety and security of journalists. we note the call of this assembly on member state authorities to ensure the protection of investigative journalists from any form of intimidation, defamation charges, threats or physical attacks, as well as to create a permanent financial scheme in support of independent investigative journalism. on behalf of the council, i can say that we are aware of the responsibility our governments have to protect journalists and different media freedom. we will continue with all appropriate means possible to respect and protect freedom of expression. the council held a dialogue on media pluralism and the rule of law in the digital age in november 2017. the related presidency conclusions reflected the importance of the issue and repeated the commitment by the council and the member states to secure a safe working environment for journalists as part of their duty to uphold fundamental rights, democracy and the rule of law.
member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, this is an important opportunity to recall and mark this day, to recall its origins that have just been set out, and to underline what it stands for. we believe freedom of expression is a fundamental human right that should apply for everyone, everywhere. an environment where journalists are free to report on any topic, on all platforms, without censoring themselves, is the key to media freedom. but today, journalists’ safety is not guaranteed, even – as we just heard – in europe, as far too often journalists and media workers find themselves attacked, persecuted, harassed or intimidated for carrying out their work. again, we’ve just heard some striking figures: in 2018 alone, 94 journalists and media staff were killed across the globe in work-related incidents, as reported by the international federation of journalists. hundreds more have been subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention without ever having been tried in court. according to unesco, only 10% of the 930 cases of killings of journalists from 2006 to 2016 worldwide have as yet been resolved. impunity for these crimes – getting away with these crimes – multiplies their impact. it erodes democratic societies by fuelling fear, mistrust and anxiety. so what are we trying to do about this? respect for freedom of expression is integrated in all our policies and our development programmes. the eu provides support and legal assistance via the mechanism for human rights defenders, a network that delivers fast response for human rights defenders under threat, including covering journalists. the eu also supports the european centre for press and media freedom and the media pluralism monitor. in 2019 a series of pilot projects will foster cooperation between journalists and self-regulatory bodies, fund cross-border investigative journalism and increase support for journalists who find themselves under threat. the commission has proposed to include a dedicated budget in the next mff as part of the creative europe programme. the commission has also spearheaded work to counter online incitement to violence and hatred by means of the code of conduct on combating illegal hate speech. on this too, the eu is currently transposing new legislative provisions in the directive on audiovisual media services. in these and other ways, we consistently stand up for the themes symbolised by this day, and we oppose, in bilateral contacts with third countries, as well as in multilateral and regional discussions, any legislation, regulation or political pressure that does not respect international human rights standards on freedom of expression. simply proclaiming the right to freedom of expression is not enough – it is not sufficient. states must also fulfil their obligation to protect freedom of expression and the safety of journalists by providing an enabling legal environment, by taking criminal threats against journalists seriously, and by vigorously prosecuting actual attacks. as has just been recalled, the recent assassinations of investigative journalist daphne caruana galizia and ján kuciak, and indeed of the saudi national, jamal khashoggi, show, sadly, that no part of the world is immune to such crimes. the commission recently highlighted the fundamental role of journalists and free and pluralistic media in promoting and upholding the rule of law in its communication on strengthening the rule of law within the union of july this year. and again, on the actual international day, on 2 november, in her declaration, the high representative paid tribute to all those who lost their lives and suffered attacks in the exercise of their freedom of expression online and offline. the eu firmly condemns the increase in crimes against journalists, both offline and online in cyberspace. the commission, on the particular case that's already been raised, has called on the maltese authorities, in the case of mrs caruana galizia, to ensure that justice is done. after all, a functioning democracy cannot thrive without free, diverse and independent media. madam president, honourable members, thank you for the opportunity to discuss this very important theme today.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, the december european council will be marked by a change of the guards, so to speak. it will be the first meeting to be chaired by president charles michel and, pending your approval of the new commission tomorrow, it will also be the first one for ms ursula von der leyen in her capacity as president of the commission, and for the new high representative, mr josep borrell. the agenda will be dominated by two pressing issues – climate change and the multiannual financial framework. let me start with climate change. you will all recall that in june the european council came close to an agreement on climate neutrality by 2050. however, a few member states felt they needed more time to assess the efforts and costs linked to the transition to climate neutrality before committing to such ambitious targets. the european council therefore asked the council and the commission to advance work on the conditions, incentives and the enabling framework, and pledged to finalise its guidance before the end of the year with a view to the adoption and submission of the eu’s long-term strategy to the united nations framework convention on climate change in early 2020. in december, the european council will aim to commit the eu to reaching climate neutrality by 2050 and identify the enabling framework that will allow us to reach that objective. the presidency has worked intensively with other member states and the commission in order to facilitate this decision. the discussion in this plenary yesterday again highlighted the need for the eu to act decisively in order to remain a world leader in climate issues. this brings me to the second topic on the european council agenda: the multiannual financial framework (mff). the finnish presidency will submit a finalised negotiation box with figures prepared on the basis of the exchange of views that took place in council preparatory bodies, as well as bilateral discussions with all delegations. we intend to submit the negotiation box in the coming few days. we are nearing the end stage of negotiations. i believe it’s in all our interest to reach an agreement on the next mff soon in order to make sure our citizens, regions, farmers, universities and other beneficiaries can continue their work uninterrupted. the presidency’s job in this respect has not been easy, the individual positions being wide apart. with the brexit cut. the status quo is not an option. we will have to pay more and, unfortunately, some will have to receive less. the leaders’ discussion therefore should identify the most important issues and prepare the ground for the future compromise. i am glad to say we have had many fruitful exchanges with parliament during the course of this the positions of parliament and the council converge in several important areas. first of all, the next mff should be able to deliver on the policies set out in the strategic agenda – ambition on climate policy, commitment to just transition, increasing the investments to research and development and a comprehensive management of migration are just a few key policies the next mff will be able to address. as in the commission proposal, the presidency is committed to renewing and modernising the eu budget by giving modern programmes the largest share of eu funds. however, we also note the importance of cohesion policy to the unity and success of the union, as well as the need to devote sufficient funds to our farmers so that they can continue to develop sustainable agriculture. the madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, despite the request of over 100 member states of the world trade organization, the appellate body for the settlement of disputes will cease to function on 10 december, and with it a serious blow to the credibility of these institutions. behind a seemingly very technical story lies a political and ideological clash: the conflict between supporters, even if critical, of the multilateral system and those who want to dismantle the international governance that has been built up over many years. the wto is clearly not working. the multilateral agenda has been almost fixed for some time, with the result that bilateral agreements have multiplied. but the trump administration's decision to block a body essential to the functioning of the wto is part of a policy that wants a system of international relations based on the law of the strongest and ideological protectionism. but let us beware of this dangerous drift, for it risks turning back the clock of history. the complexity of globalisation processes requires effective but shared rules to protect citizens who call for more democratic and transparent decision-making processes and to protect businesses who call for uniform global rules and standards to increase trade and exports. either international trade will help make our societies fairer and our economies more sustainable or it will become just a political tool for the populist of the day to use and consume.
madam president, it is very important for the eu to boost exports and jobs, and that we have free, fair and reciprocal trade relations with the rest of the world. trade policy is a great example of how important the eu is in the multilateral order. that’s why it’s very unfortunate that the wto appellate body is set to become dysfunctional in two weeks’ time. but we should have a look at and bear in mind the context in which the us is blocking the appointment of the new judges and why. the wto ruling, as it functions today, has not prevented china from using massive state aid and forced technology transfer to compete unfairly also with us, the eu. the commission proposal to set up a new global trade court – together with countries such as china – to replace the wto appellate body, would then be problematic. wouldn’t we then undermine the important joint efforts – in which the us and japan are with us – in the reforming of the wto? a new court could easily become a permanent solution and lessen efforts in the wto reform. let’s rather have temporary bilateral arrangements on the wto ruling, like deals we have with canada and norway already.

(applause)we sometimes forget that our greatest achievements have always come when we are bold. we were bold when we sought peace where there was pain. we were bold when we created a single market and a single currency. we were bold when we welcomed the part of our european family that had been out in the cold for too long. but in the last years, we have had to focus on the here and now, managing crisis after emergency, fighting to keep our unity and solidarity intact. if we have emerged stronger in that time – and i believe we have – it is, in great part, thanks to the leadership and conviction of my predecessor, jean-claude juncker. a great european, he has devoted his heart, his soul and his life to our union, and his legacy speaks for itself. jean—claude, merci de nous tous. (sustained applause) monsieur le président, mesdames et messieurs les membres du parlement européen, cela fait quatre mois que vous m’avez accordé votre confiance. depuis, j’ai rencontré tous les groupes politiques et tous les chefs d’état ou de gouvernement. ensemble, nous avons formé une équipe européenne exceptionnelle. vous, les membres du parlement, avez auditionné chacun d’entre nous. je vous avais promis de vous écouter, c’est exactement ce que j’ai fait, et je continuerai de le faire, accompagnée de maros šefčovič et de tous les autres membres du collège. nous avons souvent été d’accord et, parfois nous ne l’avons pas été, mais c’est la démocratie à l’œuvre. aujourd’hui, ici, au cœur de cette démocratie européenne, je vous demande votre soutien pour un nouveau départ de l’europe. the team you are voting on today come from different cultures and countries and have different backgrounds and political colours. we have teachers and farmers, mayors and ministers, doctors and diplomats, engineers and entrepreneurs. we have those born before the berlin wall was built and those born after it was torn down, those who lived in dictatorships and those who helped young democracies join our union. it is a team with almost – almost – as many women as men, only one woman away from gender balance. (applause)this shows we have made real progress, but also that we still have to do more. as the first woman to be president of the commission, every member of my college will have a gender-balanced cabinet – for the very first time. (applause)this is an unsettled world, where too many powers only speak the language of confrontation and unilateralism, but it is also a world where millions of people are taking to the streets to protest against corruption or to demand democratic change. the world needs our leadership more than ever: to keep engaging with the world as a responsible power, and to be a force for peace and for positive change. we must show our partners at the united nations that they can rely on us as a champion of multilateralism. we must demonstrate to our friends in the western balkans that we share the same continent, the same history, the same culture, and we will share the same destiny. our door remains open. (applause)we also share the same destiny with our transatlantic partners. yes, we have issues – without any doubt. but our ties have lasted the test of time. while we are speaking, thousands of students, researchers, entrepreneurs and artists continue to build zillions of friendships, business contacts, and science projects. this myriad of fine threads woven together make a bond that is stronger than any individual point of discord. countries from east to west, from south to north, need europe to be a true partner. we can be the shapers of a better global order. this is europe’s vocation and it’s what european citizens want. i am happy to have such an experienced diplomat as josep borrell on our team, working alongside jutta urpilainen, olivér várhelyi and janez lenarčič. they will do an invaluable job together. we will invest in alliances and coalitions to advance our values. we will promote and protect europe’s interest through open and fair trade. we’ll strengthen our partners through cooperation because strong partners make europe strong too. my commission will not be afraid to speak the language of confidence, but it will be our way, the european way. this is the geopolitical commission that i have in mind and that europe urgently needs. if there is one area where the world needs our leadership, it is on protecting our climate. this is an existential issue for europe and for the world. how can it not be existential when 85% of people in extreme poverty live in the 20 countries most vulnerable to climate change? how can it not be existential when we see venice under water, portugal’s forests on fire or lithuania’s harvests cut by half because of droughts? this has happened before, without any question, but never with that frequency and with that intensity. we do not have a moment to waste anymore on fighting climate change. (applause) the faster europe moves, the greater the advantage will be for our citizens, our competitiveness and our prosperity. the european green deal is a must for the health of our planet, our people and for our economy. frans timmermans is the right person to make this happen. (applause)and i am delighted that he will be supported by kadri simson, adina vălean and many others. the european green deal is our new growth strategy. it will help us cut emissions while creating jobs. at the core of it will be an industrial strategy that enables our businesses – big and small – to innovate and to develop new technologies, while creating new markets. we will be global standard setters. this is our competitive advantage and is the best way to ensure a level-playing field. but all of this has to serve the european people. they want and expect europe to act on climate and environment, but they also need affordable, clean and secure energy. they need to be skilled to work in the jobs of tomorrow. they need to commute to those new jobs or be connected from home and we have to make sure that those needs are fulfilled in a sustainable way. it is a generational transition towards climate neutrality by mid—century, but this transition must be just and inclusive or it will not happen at all. (applause)it will need massive investment in innovation, research, infrastructure, housing, and the training of people. it will require public and private investments at the european and at national levels. and, once again, europe is already leading the way. the european union will mainstream climate financing throughout its budget, but also throughout capital markets and the entire investment chain. in regions that will have to make a bigger step than most we will support people and businesses with a targeted just transition mechanism. it will cut across different funds and instruments and attract the private investment we need. to help us achieve this, the european investment bank will be a trusted partner. i am particularly happy that the progress it has made to strengthen its role as european climate bank is obvious. this will boost investment in european technologies and the solutions the world is looking for. but there is more to do. we only account for approximately 9% of global emissions. we have to bring the world with us and this is already happening. from china to canada and through to california, others are working with us on their own emissions trading system, and phil hogan will ensure that our future trade agreements include a chapter on sustainable development because we know that climate change is about all of us. we have the duty to act and the power to lead. a writer. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the subject we have chosen this afternoon for our oral question to the commission is: what is the state of play of the internal electronic market for telephone services? we have already discussed this on several occasions with many other colleagues in the committee on the internal market. the subject of this afternoon's debate is a very local one here in the strasbourg area. a german citizen told me that his mother-in-law was in hospital in strasbourg and that he had not been able to call her during her stay there because the hospital there kindly offered a free service number for french citizens, which was not available from another european country, which in this situation was only a few kilometres away. i think, commissioner gabriel, that we must deal with the question in a very specific way: can the european internal telecommunications market be such that, although we have abolished crossborder roaming charges, citizens can no longer call their in-laws in a neighbouring country simply because of a 0800 number? in my view, this is indisputable, because the advantage of the 0800 number is precisely that it should be easy for citizens to call - free of charge - and if it is impossible to do so across borders, we have done a disservice to the european single market. i would therefore like to know from the commission - and i would like to know from all the members present this afternoon - what we can do to correct this error, to ensure that not only does the bill for crossborder calls remain low, but that crossborder accessibility is also reliably solved for service numbers. it is therefore important that the european commission gives us a clear answer here. this evil must be removed.
member of the commission. madam president, first of all, i would like to thank the members of the european parliament for drawing our attention to this important issue. the european commission considers it important to guarantee access to the 0 800 number. we will look at this in detail, first because - as you have just rightly said, mr schwab - this is a crucial issue for the completion of the digital single market. companies generally use 0 800 numbers to provide better service to their customers. this is often a decision to help in a way that is easier and more effective. in the case of a toll-free 0 800 number, the cost of the call is passed on to the called party, for example a company with a customer service telephone. in order to avoid any risk of fraud and to protect the caller from the high costs of calls from abroad, especially for small ngos such as the cancer helpline, national and european legislation does not prohibit callers from rejecting calls from abroad. so far, it is clear that we have not received many complaints, but i do not trust that. it is not a question of whether there are many or few, we are talking about something essential and concrete. i would therefore like to see what other means we have at our disposal. draw your attention to the directive establishing the new european electronic communications code. you remember, we adopted it last year. the new code introduced a number of measures aimed specifically at combating crossborder distortions and eliminating their effects. it is therefore clear that the code will contribute to the completion of the single market. it is currently scheduled to enter into force in december 2020, and the commission is working closely with member states to help them implement it. of course, the european parliament is always welcome in this process. we will have the same objective: to ensure that the new measures established by the code are operational after december next year, and we will monitor them closely. we shall therefore continue to follow this matter. the completion of the digital single market is a top priority and we are already well advanced. we now have a set of policies, investment measures and regulatory initiatives that have given european businesses important tools for digital competitiveness and, at the same time, strengthened user rights. as you know, we have abolished roaming charges throughout the european union. recently we introduced reduced rates for international calls within the member states. these two measures have contributed greatly to making european consumers feel that they are concerned by a genuine digital single market policy. at this stage, i can assure you that the commission will continue to monitor closely the development of the situation with access to the 0800 number and it is on this basis that further measures will be taken, depending - i repeat - on the development of the situation. today's debate is also a contribution for which we thank you.

the single market. an example of such a measure is the introduction of single maximum union-wide voice termination rates by a delegated act which the commission shall adopt by the end of next year. we may be the last generation that can still act and have an impact and make a difference. we only simply have a couple of decades left. and at the same time, for the epp it is also clear that you don’t put a man – or a woman, for that matter – on the moon by just banning things, by increasing taxes and by telling people what they must do or what they can no longer do. we do it by bringing the best and the brightest together – that first of all. we need ground-breaking research: the smartest solutions and the cleanest industry which will provide jobs for europeans and opportunities. let europe be the continent that develops and produces alternative aircraft fuels while also improving the rail market for shorter distances. let europe be the continent where we produce co2-low or even -free steel. we in the epp might not be climate warriors, but we are – and we need to be – climate nerds. that is what europe needs to get ahead. we do it, secondly, by leaving nobody behind, it has been said; by not putting the burden, for example, on those who can least afford it. and this is a real worry among europeans. we do it by working with our farmers and foresters: farmland and forests take up more than three quarters of our surface in europe, and some brand farmers and foresters as the villains, as the problem in this debate, whereas they’re part of the solution. and we should help them, starting by ensuring them a fair price for their products as well as an international level playing field. and thirdly, we do it by bringing by being coherent and consistent. for the epp it is clear that an ambitious climate policy and a smart industrial policy need to go hand in hand. a green deal without a good deal for our industry will not deliver the change that we are looking for. we want and we need ambition with the business case. and finally, we need a global, level playing field, it has been said, ensuring that other parts of the world either play along or cannot have uncorrected access to the european market. today is a day, i think, for firmly putting that dot on the horizon. we agree on the direction that we are heading in. we share an ambition. but the work on how we get there is only starting. let’s not fool ourselves. it will be challenging, and what we need is a combination of real vision and practical strategy, and this is what the epp can and will deliver.

pillar, which implements the united nations' 2030 agenda and the sustainable development goals. in this respect, we welcome the fact that the proposal fulfils our longstanding aspiration to in writing. – farmers are the first to feel the impact of climate change. yet bear in mind the pressure on their shoulders by the rigorous standards of the future cap, the budget cuts, the unfair competition triggered by the mercosur trade agreement and the international trade disputes countermeasures. it is, thus, fundamental to design policies that accompany our farmers towards this transition, instead of putting even more pressure on them. forestry also plays a crucial role in addressing climate change. it has significant potential to reduce emissions, sequester carbon and boost economies in a sustainable manner. with over 40% of the eu’s land area covered by forests, it is clear that the european green deal must include an updated post-2020 eu forest strategy, to put the legislation in line with renewed climate and biodiversity ambitions. however, as the commission knows, each member states has its specificities. during the last plenary debate on the protection of forests, romanian illegal logging was discussed. i call on the commission to explain all the concrete initiatives which might be taken in order to protect romanian forests and its biodiversity.
the european commission's communication launching the european green deal reinforces the coherence and relevance of a progressive, inclusive and sustainable agenda to address the climate emergency and to give the european union a leading role in the energy transition and the implementation of the 2030 agenda. the just transition mechanism to be presented at the beginning of 2020 should allow no region, territory or sector to be left behind in achieving the objectives. i also stress the importance of the commitment to present a new industrial strategy and a 'climate law' in the first half of 2020, which will make the emission reduction target more ambitious. the option of applying a carbon tax under wto rules is a sign that the financial leverage of the pact will not jeopardise the financing of cohesion and convergence policies. the european union cannot hesitate to adopt a practice which will also be an inspiration to the rest of the world. the political decision-makers and civil society must be mobilised. in this context, the european commission's decision to present the green deal first to the european parliament has important political significance.

on behalf of the epp group. madam president, first of all i would like to thank my fellow meps, the parliamentary groups, who have agreed that this debate should take place in the epicentre of european democracy. today we celebrate 30 years, exactly today, since timisoara erupted in a seemingly banal incident on december 16, 1989. on december 17th, ceausescu's murderous regime was shooting at the population through the people's army. the revolution spread from timisoara to all cities of the country. millions of romanians were in the streets. the brutality of the regime was materialized in over 1,142 romanians shot, 3,200 romanians wounded, 700 romanians tortured. however, any of the millions of romanians who took to the streets were facing the bullets of the romanian army turned against their own people. the romanians' desire to return to a europe of values, from which they were snatched by soviet tanks, was much stronger than their fear of repression. it is a moment when romanians said decisively, with the sacrifice of their lives, "no" to communism and returned to the european family. today they're in nato, they're in europe, they're where they belong. i would like to conclude by saying that the european union is not only about peace in europe, the european union is also about the prohibition of dictatorships on the territory of the european union.
the european parliament has been asked to vote on the report by the committee on budgets, which is to be submitted to the european parliament by the end of the year. unlike other former communist countries, the return from communism to democracy in romania was made through human sacrifice. over a thousand people have died for freedom and thousands more have been injured. the thousands of human sacrifices in december 1989 are in addition to the hundreds of thousands of romanians of all ethnicities and confessions in romania, who since the establishment of communism in romania in 1946, have fought and campaigned for the defense of freedom, democracy and fundamental human rights. many of them fought with weapons in hand as partisans in the mountains, others were imprisoned by the communists and died in unsanitary prisons, and others went into exile. thousands more romanians were shot at the romanian border as they tried to escape westward from the great prison that the communists had turned romania into. because of its refusal to serve the communist party, the greek catholic church in romania was outlawed in 1948, and its bishops, along with hundreds of priests and thousands of faithful, were thrown into prisons, where many died. along with greek catholic priests, orthodox priests, protestant and non-protestant pastors, and even people of no particular faith and of different ethnicities were imprisoned in communist prisons because they refused to serve the communist party or opposed communist ideology. added to this are millions of romanian families whose land and other property was confiscated by the communist state, destroying their livelihoods. the 1989 romanian revolution was the culmination of a 40-year struggle to restore freedom and democracy in romania. 30 years after the anti-communist revolution, we commemorate this event and we are glad that all the representatives of romania in this parliament are joining hands to carry forward freedom for themselves and for the generations that will come after us.

madam president, personally, as a man who has lived half his life under an oppressive regime, i believe that there is nothing more dangerous and humiliating for a human being than dictatorship. i also think that the distance between democracy and dictatorship is sometimes only a split second, that split second when you choose to be silent rather than speak. the victims of the revolution were killed by bullets, but in fact, their tragic fate was decided by the murderous silence of those who worked for or indulged in the oppressive system for their own peace and benefit. it's good that the truth of 1989 is known. but in addition, it is our duty to be careful and to speak loudly, firmly, in time, so that we can save those people whom we would otherwise be paying tribute to post mortem. let's all be on the lookout for the first signs of dictatorship, because today it's much more subtle, sometimes hiding behind a democratic veneer and able to pervert by manipulating even the brightest minds. a form of dictatorship begins to build itself when you discover that you can no longer assert your political choice without being verbally assaulted and isolated, including by your circle of friends and family, or when your country is ideologically divided into two camps ready to tear each other apart until there is only one left. so the truth is important, but we also have to see the signs and in that critical split second choose to speak.

physical presence. this concerns the reallocation of taxing rights, the so-called pillar 1. two: to address new forms of excessive tax competition under what is called pillar 2. to address those challenges and reach an ambitious global agreement, we then need to find a global solution that effectively captures digital business models, notably those operating in jurisdictions without a physical presence, and to put a floor on excessive international tax competition and close remaining beps loopholes. in addition, while working on a global solution at international level, our aim is it is important to understand the economic impact of the options proposed under both pillars, so that member states can take an informed decision. the preliminary results of our economic analysis on revenues are, until now, encouraging. they suggest that the eu as a whole could benefit under pillar 1 and that all member states would benefit from pillar 2. the commission has now asked member how it should be implemented at eu level. if no or limited agreement is reached internationally by 2020, it is crystal clear that the strong rationale for eu action at eu level will remain and that the commission will act on this basis.

madam president, what happened in the black sea port is undoubtedly a tragedy and we must take all measures to ensure that this does not happen again. at the same time, however, i do not think that the romanian farmer should be the one to pay because, in this incident, he has absolutely no fault. on the contrary, the romanian farmer breeds his animals according to the highest standards imposed by the common agricultural policy and not only that, but his subsidies are conditional on this. secondly, i can assure you that no farmer in the world who has invested energy, time and money in raising their animals does not send them to export with the thought that they will end up in terrible conditions. third, the romanian farmer often encounters insurmountable obstacles when trying to sell his products on the european market or even in hypermarkets in his own country. as things stand, the non-eu states are, at this point, his only chance of survival. the solution, then, is not to stop the export of live animals, but to tighten the rules we impose on third countries, especially when it comes to long-distance transport, to monitor closely compliance with these rules, to ensure and encourage the slaughter of animals in the country of origin, because we have the trade in meat, which would bring more benefits to both the farmer and the livestock sector and the country.
madam president, millions of citizens saw the gruesome pictures of the ship carrying 40 000 sheep sinking off the coast of romania. this is not the first time, and i’m afraid it will not be the last time, that this has happened. but let’s be honest: would the alternative for these sheep have been any better, being stuck on a cold ship for weeks in their thousands, left in their own dirt and thrown overboard when they die of hunger or exhaustion? whom are we kidding here? the mass export of live animals will never be able to guarantee good animal welfare conditions. we need to stop this absurd and cruel business model. let’s stop subsidising intensive animal agriculture, which produces so many animals, we don’t know where to ship them any more. let’s work towards a ban on the transport of live animals to third countries. the eu’s inaction is growing more and more obvious by the day, and we need to act fast if we don’t want citizens to lose all faith in us.

madam president, i understand your concerns and support the establishment of slaughterhouses, particularly in areas where they are lacking. i would like to ask you what the short-term consequences would be of banning the transport of live animals from the european union. first of all, it would mean famines in certain parts of the world -- and i say this clearly -- famines because of the lack of certain products. on the other hand, it means the bankruptcy of farmers, who would no longer have markets to sell. recent data has confirmed that these phenomena -- bankruptcies and famines -- lead to desperate acts, whether it's farmer suicides or migrants shipwrecked in the mediterranean. i believe that, in addition to animal welfare, we must take a rational stance and give priority to the interests of human beings when making any decision. let's check the transporters, the way they transport live animals over the sea because otherwise australia, new zealand, argentina...
