in writing. for 10 years we have hoped that the lisbon treaty could strengthen the rights of national and linguistic minorities across the union. today we have come to understand the disheartening reality that even the most outrageous violations of national minorities, such as the malina hedvig case, the re-nationalizations, or the use of minority languages and symbols, have become condonable. the european commission was not at liberty to invoke its lack of competence or the competence of the member states, unless there was a political interest in upholding the rights and principles. unfortunately, in many cases today, fundamental rights have become a tool of ideological struggle and a double standard. some issues of national sovereignty, which are not in line and are almost always led by christian-conservative members, can be objected to and held accountable. however, in the case of other member states with generally left-wing liberal governments, this rigidity disappears and the finding of a permissive lack of competence remains. the double standards applied by the european commission and the european parliament over the past 10 years have destroyed the union's coherence and its belief in a common europe. so there is still a lot to be done for the future of europe!
in writing. it is now ten years since the treaty of lisbon, which established the european union, entered into force. this anniversary is of particular importance for the indigenous national and linguistic minority communities in europe, as it is the first time that legislation at eu level has established that the european union is founded on the values of respect for the rights of persons belonging to minorities. within a few years, this was followed by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which clearly states that all discrimination, including discrimination on grounds of belonging to a national minority, is prohibited and that the union respects cultural, religious and linguistic diversity. however, after ten years, it has also become clear that the actual content of these provisions has yet to be developed. the implementation of the rights of indigenous national and linguistic minorities faces difficulties in many eu member states and these principles are not reflected in eu legislation. so it's very important that the next ten years don't go to waste. the consultation on the future of europe and the minority safe-pack initiative provide a good opportunity and a basis for the next anniversary to commemorate specific eu legislation and key content beyond the basic principles, in order to finally give indigenous national and linguistic minorities their rights.
in writing. as the eu celebrates the 10th anniversary of the lisbon treaty and the charter of fundamental rights, people can draw valuable lessons from the anti-people road to europe that has been built at their expense. the cfsp, pesco, the new intervention financing funds, have strengthened the militarisation of the eu and the aggressiveness of the european monopolies in their fierce confrontation with the other imperialist centres and powers. the treaty has armed the eu and governments with more brutal means of promoting anti-people policies: control of state budgets, the euro, memoranda of understanding, the crushing of wages and pensions. it has enlarged existing and created new mechanisms of repression (europolícia, eurogard, eurogospel, etc.), made the restriction of popular freedoms and rights more asphyxiating by strengthening anti-communism, persecutions against communist parties. it has turned the mediterranean into a watery grave for thousands of displaced refugees and migrants. the only rights that the so-called "charter" really guarantees are the "inviolable property of capitalists, the free movement of capital, the recognition of the employers' strike. the 'euro treaties' are nothing but shackles, with which the eu and governments, chain workers to the interests of capital. the people have the power to free themselves from the tyranny of the monopolies, by breaking free from the eu and nato, by taking power and the economy, by building the europe of socialism.
in writing. the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon 10 years ago was undeniably a major step towards closer european cooperation among people. more democratic institutional functioning, stronger rights for eu citizens, a further move of the eu from mere economic cooperation towards european cooperation that puts citizens first. citizens belonging to indigenous national minorities looked with confidence at developments 10 years ago. they hoped that it would also bring positive changes in the protection of minorities in the eu. the lisbon treaty has made the concept of a national minority part of eu primary law. article 2 of the treaty lists respect for the rights of persons belonging to minorities among the values of the union, and article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights prohibits discrimination on grounds of language and national minority. since then, apart from the solemn declaration, not much has happened. the eu's enforcement of minority rights continues to face obstacles. so, in terms of minority rights, we've lost another decade. many questions remain unanswered in the field. the lisbon treaty will only deliver on its promises if the union takes more positive and concrete steps to protect minorities. our task is nothing less than to listen to the citizens, to fulfil the 10-year promise and to establish as soon as possible appropriate eu standards for the protection of indigenous minorities.

against the climate threat - i am pleased to announce that the european council has unanimously reached an agreement on the 2050 climate neutrality target, providing a longer deadline for a european country to implement this agreement, which was unanimously supported. it's a giant step in the right direction, and it allows for progress on what i've called, along with other projects, the men and women on the moon project. i think we do need to set a course and an ambition. it is done through this commitment. i would also like to emphasize that the european council has rightly, in my view, stated that this climate transition must be equitable, socially balanced and requires financial means. we have noted the european investment bank's announcement of very high ambition in terms of starting point, that there are national situations which are not exactly the same. we also noted the importance, in our view, of having a strategy that respects the choice of individual member states madam president, i remember very well what the word foreign agent meant in the former socialist czechoslovakia and in the whole of the central and eastern european bloc under the soviet dictatorship. it was simply a label for dissidents, for those who fought for human rights, for freedom and democracy in countries like czechoslovakia, poland, hungary and other countries. today, the russian ministry of justice uses the term to target undesirable organizations and individuals, such as journalists. the czech organization people in need was also included in the list of such organizations. the organisation is the largest non-profit organisation in the czech republic and central europe, providing human rights, development aid and education in more than thirty countries worldwide. in russia, the organization people in need has supported independent journalists, civil society and has also provided assistance to political dissidents. it is therefore absolutely unacceptable that a respected independent organization from a member state of the european union is considered an undesirable foreign agent in the russian federation. therefore, i fully support the proposal to repeal this law in russia.

vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, the european union has a long-standing and clear position on russia’s ‘foreign agent’ law, and the newest amendment to this law, signed by president putin on 2 december, widens the scope of the ‘foreign agent media’ law to include individuals. many of you have expressed your strong concern about that – and, i think, rightly, because this has the potential to affect independent journalists and bloggers and is another step towards restricting media freedom and freedom of expression in russia. since 2012, when the ‘foreign agent’ law was first introduced in russia, enabling non-government organisations to be branded as foreign agents, about 150 ngos had this label imposed on them. they have been subject to fines, inspections and stigmatisation. the impact has been to restrict fundamental freedom in russia, consume the scarce resources of ngos, and inhibit independent civil society in the country. in 2017, foreign agent legislation expanded, so that any media organisation receiving foreign funding, either directly or indirectly, could be labelled as a foreign agent. it has again reduced the space for free and independent media, as well as independent voices. ‘foreign agent’ legislation goes against russia’s human rights obligations and commitments. the eu has repeatedly condemned this legislation, most recently in a statement by the external action service – the spokesperson on 23 november: the extension of the law to include private individuals is yet another move to curb freedom of expression. we will continue to call on the russian authorities to respect their international obligations on freedom of association and freedom of speech. it is essential that russian citizens are able to exercise freedom of association, including the right to join and participate in non-governmental organisations which promote the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. the european union will continue to support russian human rights activists and civil society as we do worldwide, because this is a fundamental principle of the european union. our support is important, be it public statements, attending trials, supporting meetings with them. we will keep monitoring developments in russia, calling the authorities to account when they do not respect fundamental rights enshrined in their constitution. we will insist on the need to respect the decisions of the european court of human rights and, in general, the council of europe conventions. that’s democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights. (applause)
ladies and gentlemen, today the court of justice of the european union delivered a judgment in case c-502/19 junqueras vies. it is a very important judgment which directly affects the composition of this institution. we didn't waste time or keep you waiting for the sake of keeping you waiting. the court held that the assumption of parliamentary mandate is the result of the votes of the electors. the court held that a person whose election to the european parliament has been officially proclaimed by the competent authority of the member state in which that election took place acquires from that moment the status of member of parliament and enjoys the protection of parliamentary immunity under article 9 of the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european union from the moment of the official proclamation of the results. consequently, the membership of parliament must be regarded as having been acquired by the mere fact and from the time of the aforementioned proclamation. the court also held that immunity entailed that the precautionary detention measure to which the elected member was subjected should be lifted in order to allow the member to go to the european parliament and complete the necessary formalities. that being said, if the competent national authority considers that the measure in question should be maintained after the person concerned has become a member of the european parliament, it must, in accordance with article 9 of the said protocol, apply to the european parliament as soon as possible for the waiver of that immunity. i call on the competent spanish authorities to comply with the judgment and have instructed parliament's services to assess as soon as possible the application of the judgment's effects on the composition of our parliament. i would inform you that i will not accept any references to the rules of procedure on this subject.

madam president. i had the privilege of watching a lot of the romanian revolution in bucharest. i was 18 years old. it was my gap year. i saw most of it through the windows of a pub called hanul lui manuc, because it was the only place in that city where you could get beer. it was a pub that brewed its own beer. the only things you could buy in bucharest at that time were italian vermouth and plum jam. it is an extraordinary thing to see the strides made by romania since then. but it’s worth remembering that the revolution, not only in romania but in the other soviet satellites, was primarily about the end of foreign occupation and the restoration of national sovereignty. yes, of course, it was about democracy, the rule of law and personal freedom, but the peoples of those countries understood that those things are meaningless unless you have mechanisms to hold your rulers to account, and that is why, as charles de gaulle observed many years ago, national sovereignty and democracy are the same thing.
madam chairman, like colleague hannan, i watched this revolution on television. it was just a few kilometers from my home in sofia, and for the first time we saw the events that were happening on the streets of bucharest, timisoara, and other romanian cities. at that time, romania was closed, as was bulgaria, and it was under a communist dictatorship. a dictatorship that tried to destroy the memory of our peoples, a dictatorship that tried to destroy our national self-consciousness, to invent some other man - a citizen of the soviet bloc, a soviet citizen. fortunately, that didn't happen, fortunately, that dictatorship collapsed. the fall of the dictatorship in romania, the events we watched on television, the battles on the outskirts of bucharest, inspired many bulgarians to change, which also succeeded in overthrowing the communist dictatorship in bulgaria and enabled our peoples to take their destiny in hand again. congratulations to all who participated in these events and warm congratulations to the brotherly romanian people!
